requirements.title: Mandatory federal toy safety standard (ASTM F963)
evidence: Third-party lab test report against the applicable ASTM F963 sections
Children's Product Certificate listing this rule
requirements.plain_english: Toys made for children under 14 generally have to meet the mandatory federal toy safety standard, which covers far more than chemicals: mechanical and physical hazards, small parts, sharp points and edges, magnets, cords and elastics, sound levels, projectiles, and how securely the battery compartment closes. Which sections apply depends on what your toy actually is and does, so this is not a single pass/fail test. Testing only for lead and phthalates is the most common way importers miss this.
requirements.self_check_hint: Ask your lab which ASTM F963 sections they tested against, and check the report names the current edition (F963-23 for toys made on or after 20 April 2024). A report citing an older edition may not be enough.

incorporated_standard.name: ASTM F963
incorporated_standard.note: 16 CFR 1250 incorporates ASTM F963 by reference. F963-23 applies to toys manufactured on or after 20 April 2024. The CFR part can point at a new edition without the CFR text itself changing, so the edition needs watching separately.

requirements.title: Children's Product Certificate (CPC)
evidence: Children's Product Certificate issued by the US importer
Underlying CPSC-accepted third-party lab test reports
requirements.plain_english: Products made for children 12 and under generally need a Children's Product Certificate before import. Worth knowing who issues it: you do, as the US importer - not your supplier and not the lab. You issue it based on passing test results, and where a children's product safety rule requires it, that testing has to come from a CPSC-accepted third-party laboratory. The certificate has to name the product, every rule it certifies against, who is keeping the records, where and when it was made and tested, and each lab involved. This appears to apply because you told us it's used by kids.
requirements.self_check_hint: A generic factory test report is not a CPC. Check the certificate is issued in your name, names the exact SKU, and lists each rule it covers - and that the test report behind it traces to the production lot you actually imported.

requirements.title: Lead limits in paint & surface coatings
evidence: Lab test report covering each paint or surface coating
requirements.plain_english: Paint and similar surface coatings on children's products have their own lead limit, separate from the lead in the material underneath. This catches things people forget to test: screen printing, decals, inks, and decorative coatings are all surface coatings.
requirements.self_check_hint: Check the lab tested each coloured coating, not just the base material - and that decals and printed graphics were included.

cfr.label: Ban of Lead-Containing Paint and Certain Consumer Products Bearing Lead-Containing Paint

requirements.title: Total lead content in accessible parts
evidence: Lab test report per accessible component, with a component map
requirements.plain_english: Separately from paint, the material a children's product is made of has a total lead limit, and it applies to each accessible component rather than to the product as an average. Clasps, zippers, charms, fasteners and solder are where this usually goes wrong, because a test on the main plastic or main metal says nothing about them.
requirements.self_check_hint: Ask for results per accessible component, with a component map - not one figure for the whole product. A supplier material declaration on its own is not a test result.

requirements.title: Phthalate limits in children's toys
evidence: Lab test report covering each accessible plasticized component
requirements.plain_english: Children's toys have limits on specified phthalates, and the limits bite on accessible plasticized parts rather than on the whole product. Watch the soft bits that are easy to overlook - vinyl decals, grips, inks, artificial leather, tubing and flexible coatings.
requirements.self_check_hint: First ask whether your product is actually a toy or a child-care article. If it is, check the report covers every accessible plasticized component, not only the obvious soft PVC.

cfr.label: Prohibition of Children's Toys and Child Care Articles Containing Specified Phthalates

requirements.title: Phthalate limits in child-care articles
evidence: Lab test report covering each accessible plasticized component
requirements.plain_english: Child-care articles - things that help a child aged 3 or under sleep, feed, suck or teethe - have limits on specified phthalates on their accessible plasticized parts. This is narrower than "anything for a child": it turns on what the article is for, so a teether or a feeding bottle is in scope where a t-shirt is not.
requirements.self_check_hint: First check whether the article really is for sleeping, feeding, sucking or teething by a child of 3 or under. If it is, check the report covers every accessible plasticized component.

cfr.label: Prohibition of Children's Toys and Child Care Articles Containing Specified Phthalates

requirements.title: Tracking label on product & packaging
evidence: Production sample or artwork showing a permanent mark on product and packaging
requirements.plain_english: Children's products need a permanent tracking label (manufacturer, date/batch, source) on the product and packaging.
requirements.self_check_hint: Look at a production sample photo - is the label molded/printed on?

requirements.title: Small parts & choking hazards
evidence: Small-parts test report, run after the use-and-abuse conditioning
Choking-hazard warning artwork where the product is for older children
requirements.plain_english: Products for children under 3 must not have small parts that could be swallowed, and the test is done after the product has been through simulated rough handling - not on a pristine sample. For older children, some toys with small parts, balls, marbles or balloons need a specific choking-hazard warning instead of being banned outright.
requirements.self_check_hint: Check the lab conditioned the sample first - drop, torque, tension, compression - and then tested for small parts. A pass on an untouched sample does not mean much if a knob twists off.

cfr.label: Method for Identifying Toys and Other Articles Intended for Use by Children Under 3 Years of Age Which Present Choking, Aspiration, or Ingestion Hazards
Hazardous substances and articles; 1500.19 and 1500.121 cover choking-hazard warnings

requirements.title: Loose or separable magnets
evidence: Magnet flux-index test report, or evidence the magnet is not loose or separable
requirements.plain_english: Small strong magnets are one of the most dangerous things in consumer products: swallowing two of them can pull the intestines together and cause life-threatening injuries. There is a federal safety standard for products containing loose or separable magnets, and it matters whether the magnet can come free at all.
requirements.self_check_hint: Ask whether any magnet can be freed by the use-and-abuse testing. If it can, ask your lab for the flux-index result against the magnet standard, not just a statement that magnets are glued in.

requirements.title: Electrically operated toys
evidence: Test report against the electrically operated toy requirements
requirements.plain_english: A toy that runs on electricity has its own set of federal requirements on top of the general toy rules - things like surface temperature, wiring, and the labelling and instructions that have to come with it. This is separate from the FCC side, which is about radio interference rather than safety.
requirements.self_check_hint: Check the report covers the electrical requirements specifically, not only the mechanical toy tests, and that the required markings are on the production artwork.

cfr.label: Requirements for Electrically Operated Toys or Other Electrically Operated Articles Intended for Use by Children

requirements.title: Toy & imitation firearm marking
evidence: Production artwork or sample showing the required blaze-orange marking
requirements.plain_english: Toy, look-alike and imitation firearms have to carry a specific permanent marking so they are not mistaken for real weapons. Note that some states and cities go further than the federal rule.
requirements.self_check_hint: Check the marking is the required type and permanently applied on the production sample - a removable sticker or a printed box does not satisfy it.

cfr.label: Marking of Toy, Look-Alike, and Imitation Firearms

requirements.title: Filing your certificate data at entry
evidence: Certificate data elements per 16 CFR 1110.11, transmitted in the ACE entry filing
For mail shipments: the same data entered in CPSC's Product Registry before arrival
requirements.plain_english: Holding a certificate is no longer enough on its own. The data from it has to be filed electronically with your customs entry, through ACE, at the time the entry is filed. Three things sellers are caught by: it applies to low-value shipments claiming the de minimis exemption as well as ordinary entries, it applies to goods withdrawn from a Foreign Trade Zone, and if the goods come in by mail the data goes into CPSC's Product Registry before arrival instead. Your customs broker normally transmits this, but only if you have given them the certificate data to transmit.
requirements.self_check_hint: Ask your customs broker directly whether they are transmitting CPSC certificate data in your entries, and confirm they hold current certificate details for each SKU. A certificate sitting in your own files does not get filed by itself - and "we've always just held the certificate" is the answer that means it is not being filed.

cfr.label: Certificates of Compliance; 1110.13(a)(1) requires eFiling of certificate data at entry

requirements.title: Art materials - chronic hazard review & labelling
evidence: Written determination by a qualified toxicologist that the formulation was reviewed
Conforming label statement, and any required chronic-hazard warnings
requirements.plain_english: Art materials - crayons, paints, markers, modelling clay, chalk and similar - have to be reviewed by a qualified toxicologist for long-term health hazards before sale, and labelled according to what that review finds. This one surprises people because the review is a required step in itself: you cannot satisfy it by testing for lead alone, and a supplier simply asserting the product is non-toxic is not the review.
requirements.self_check_hint: Ask for the toxicologist's determination by name, not a generic 'non-toxic' claim or a conformity certificate. Then check the label wording matches what that determination concluded.
